catalog_quote: Enfin, il faut obseruer pour la prononciation, qu'ils prononcent la derniere syllabe fort long. Il y a aussi quelque difference entre le langage des hommes & celuy des femmes. Les hommes adjoustent quelquefois à la fin du mot, bo, ou bonne; les femmes au contraire ajoustent la particule ri; exemple, les hommes disent, ie vay à Ceperou, aou Ceperoubo, ou Ceperoubon nisan, & les femmes disent, aou Ceperiri nisan.

Les hommes adjoustent quelquefois à la fin du mot, bo, ou bonne; les femmes au contraire ajoustent la particule ri; exemple, les hommes disent, ie vay à Ceperou, aou Ceperoubo, ou Ceperoubon nisan, & les femmes disent, aou Ceperiri nisan.
new_statements.translation: Finally, it must be observed regarding pronunciation that they pronounce the last syllable very long. There is also some difference between the speech of the men and that of the women. The men sometimes add at the end of the word bo, or bonne; the women on the contrary add the particle ri; for example, the men say 'I am going to Ceperou', aou Ceperoubo or Ceperoubon nisan, and the women say aou Ceperiri nisan.

Il y a aussi quelque difference entre le langage des hommes & celuy des femmes. Les hommes adjoustent quelquefois à la fin du mot, bo, ou bonne; les femmes au contraire ajoustent la particule ri; exemple, les hommes disent, ie vay à Ceperou, aou Ceperoubo, ou Ceperoubon nisan, & les femmes disent, aou Ceperiri nisan.' This matches the reported quote word for word; the locator (Livre troisièm…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The final syllable of the word is the prominent one (Biet hears it as pronounced 'very long'); no other prosodic statement exists for the pidgin.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the same paragraph notes optional men's/women's word-final particles (-bo/-bon vs -ri), which would shift which syllable is final.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('la derniere syllabe'), as heard by a French priest in 1652-53 in words and short phrases of the trade language spoken to Frenchmen; phrased as length, not stress or accent, so it may reflect phonetic final lengthening or a French listener's perception rather than a stress rule. Glottolog and Bakker et al. 2018 treat Biet's 'Galibi' as Pidgin Carib; Biet himself calls it the language of the Galibis.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 5.1/5.3 lists zero descriptive references for pidg1256; hh.bib tags only four wordlist/ethnographic items to NOCODE_Pidgin-Carib: Boyer 1654, Biet 1664, Prudhomme 1797, Nimuendajú 1926 ("Galibi do Uaçá"). The language is known only from these European travel-book wordlists and phrase lists. The quoted statement comes from Biet 1664, which Glottolog and Bakker, Gretenkort & Parkvall (2018: 180, 184) treat as Pidgin Carib ("materials on 'Galibi', which is actually Pidgin Carib"); Biet himself calls it "la Langue des Galibis". Pelleprat 1655 (Introduction à la langue des Galibis) is tagged Galibi Carib [car] = Kali'na (gali1262) by Glottolog and called "partly pidgin" by Bakker et al; it says (p. 4) the language "n'a aucun accent rude" and (p. 13) that a rising accent on the last syllable marks a question — recorded here as context, not as the pidgin's statement. The lexifier Kali'na (Hoff 1968, OA on OAPEN, DOI 10.26530/oapen_613361) has its own stress description. Crevaux's Wayana-Carib pidgin (Bakker et al. 2018) is a separate Glottolog languoid (NOCODE_Ndyuka-Wayana-Pidgin); its phonology section (pp. 213-214) says nothing about stress.

sources.note: p. 398, last of his grammatical 'Remarques': 'Enfin, il faut obseruer pour la prononciation, qu'ils prononcent la derniere syllabe fort long' (they pronounce the last syllable very long); then notes men's vs women's word-final particles (-bo/-bon vs -ri). sources.note: §4.7 Phonology (pp. 213-214) covers only vowels, consonants and syllable shape of Crevaux's (separate) Wayana pidgin: 'There is no indication of length, nasality, glottalization, etc. for any of the vowels'; nothing on stress. §3.4 (p. 184): 'Carib Pidgin has been documented since the 1650s, in supposedly Carib ("Galibi") materials collected by Biet (1664) and Boyer (1654)'; states no thorough study of Pidgin Carib exists.

sources.note: Glottolog tags it Galibi Carib [car], Bakker et al. 2018 'partly pidgin'. p. 4 (scanned page header): the language 'est douce, &.. n'a aucun accent rude, ny prononciation gutturale'; p. 13: speakers sometimes say a single word 'auquel ils adioustent sur la derniere syllabe vn ton d'accent aigu' to make it a question (Tibouchiné -> Tibouchiné?).
